summary: S1 (Speaker 1)'s maxim can be universalised: 'argue from what anyone can check' holds as a law for everyone, while S2's maxims — misstate the other side, then dismiss the speaker — contradict themselves the moment everyone follows them.

points.title: S1's maxim: judge by checkable reasons
points.text: S1's maxim is: when defending a default, offer reasons anyone can examine (n2, n3) and grant the other side's good point (n9). Universalised, every debater does the same and debate still works; no one is used merely as a means, because each claim is left open for the other to test.

points.title: S2's maxim fails universalisability
points.text: S2's maxim in the 'never meet' move (n5) and the 'companies I know' move (n6) is: restate the other side in an extreme form, or generalise from a handful of cases, whenever it helps. Universalised, no restatement could be trusted and no sample would settle anything; the maxim contradicts the very practice of arguing it relies on.

points.title: S2's motive attack fails the humanity formula
points.text: 'You only say this because you hate commuting' (n7) uses S1 merely as a means: it bypasses S1's reasons and steers the audience by motive instead of argument. S1's reply at n9, conceding the junior-onboarding point (n8), treats S2 as an end whose reasons must be answered.
